articles.title: DHS watchdog finds immigrants held at ‘Alligator Alcatraz’ in outdoor cages the size of phone booths
articles.summary: WASHINGTON — Some immigrants detained at Florida’s now-shuttered “Alligator Alcatraz” were confined in outdoor cages only slightly larger than telephone booths for more than an hour at a time, according to a new report by the Department of Homeland Security’s inspector general.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — Some immigrants detained at Florida’s now-shuttered “Alligator Alcatraz” were confined in outdoor cages only slightly larger than telephone booths for more than an hour at a time, according to a new report by the Department of Homeland Security’s inspector general. The watchdog report marks the first time a government agency has confirmed the existence of the cramped cages at the South Florida Detention Facility. Amnesty International found in a report published in December, based on interviews with detainees and a tour of the facility, that the cages were used to punish detainees and amounted to torture, sparking a congressional probe. The inspector general’s findings don’t go as far, but the report says “the use of such restrictive spaces is highly unconventional and does not align with standards for humane treatment.” The DHS watchdog findings are a rare instance when a federal inspector general has publicly criticized the Trump administration. Since he returned to office in 2025, President Donald Trump has fired at least 18 inspectors general, who operate within federal agencies but are tasked with conducting objective audits and investigating allegations of waste, fraud and abuse of power. Homeland Security’s inspector general, Joseph Cuffari, is one of the few Cabinet-level inspectors general who wasn’t fired in the purge. DHS IG inspectors visited the facility in January as part of its Congressional mandate to inspect detention facilities. The inspector general’s report found the “small metal enclosures” were roughly 4-by-4, or 16 square feet, and facility staff members described them as “calming areas” for “detainees to de-escalate and have time alone.” The facility also had indoor cages that measured 18 square feet, the report says. The cages are less than half the size of the smallest spaces that people are supposed to be held at immigration detention facilities. ICE guidelines say rooms designed to hold one person at a time should be a minimum of 37 square feet. By comparison, solitary confinement cells at federal prisons are around 84 square feet. The detention facility, which Florida’s attorney general dubbed Alligator Alcatraz, opened in July 2025 in the Everglades and was built by Gov. Ron DeSantis’ administration. It was part of a state and federal partnership known as a 287(g) agreement, which allows state and local law enforcement agencies to carry out special immigration enforcement duties, which are otherwise a federal responsibility. ICE is to provide oversight “to ensure compliance with federal immigration law and ICE policies,” and immigration enforcement activities will be “supervised and directed by ICE,” according to 287(g) agreements between Florida agencies and ICE, which were filed in court documents in a lawsuit over the existence of the facility. Homeland Security denied that it had authority over day-to-day operations at the facility, writing in a signed response from the DHS undersecretary of management and the acting director of ICE to the inspector general’s report that ICE didn’t have a contract with the state of Florida to run Alligator Alcatraz. Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, also wrote that the 287(g) agreement doesn’t give the federal government authority over the physical operations of any detention facility. The IG report noted that ICE personnel were on site at the facility and all detainees were given an ICE handbook that said Alligator Alcatraz “is a facility of the United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement,” despite the lack of a contract to run day-to-day operations. DHS didn’t immediately respond to additional questions about the report or the agreement. DeSantis was asked about the report during his daily press conference and said he had not read it. “I know that it was inspected, all those standards,” he said of the detention facility. The goal was not to apply those standards but to exceed those standards.” DeSantis and Trump toured the facility together and described it at the time as crucial to helping in the Trump administration’s mass deportation effort. But the use of tented housing units and detainees’ vulnerability to severe weather immediately drew backlash from Democrats and immigrant advocates — and sparked a series of lawsuits that are ongoing. The facility shut down in June. DeSantis said it was always meant to be temporary, and detainees were either deported or sent to other federal facilities. Amnesty International toured the facility in September 2025 and was able to interview four detainees, finding “inhuman and unsanitary conditions,” including overflowing toilets “with fecal matter seeping into where people are sleeping,” exposure to insects and lights 24 hours a day, according to the its report on the tour. Some of the detainees interviewed for the Amnesty report also described the metal cage, which they called the “box.” “Individuals are put in the ‘box’, their hands are shackled and their feet are attached to restraints on the ground,” the Amnesty report said. “They are unable to sit down or move positions, and are forced to remain there for hours in the heat with hardly any water or protection from the sun, heat and insects.” Amnesty concluded that “the use of the ‘box’ as a form of punishment constitutes torture.” ICE told the inspector general that the detainees were shackled when they were “escorted to the enclosures but not while in them.” Records reviewed by the inspector general showed that 79 detainees were held in the 16- and 18-square foot metal cages over the six months from July 17, 2025, to Jan. 18. The average time was just under an hour, and the longest anyone spent in one of the cages was just about two hours, according to the inspector general’s report, which relied on internal records from the facility. A sign attached to the outside of the “holding cell” said it was used to “provide a safe and secure place in the general population for detainees to reflect on their behavior choices, manage their emotions, reduce stress and practice self-directed behavior.” According to facility records included in the inspector general’s report, a detainee “may have a maximum of 2 hours to spend in the holding cell and may leave at any time, by detainee request or per staff directive.” Staffers reported that “time spent in the small metal enclosures is closely monitored, and detainees are not locked in, even though we observed locking mechanisms on them,” the inspector general’s report says. The picture of the cage included in the report shows an exterior-facing door lock similar to one used for a public restroom where a code is punched in to open it. It’s not clear whether other ICE facilities hold detainees in such close quarters. The Florida facility cost the state more than $1 billion in taxpayer money, according to state records made public in a lawsuit. The Federal Emergency Management Agency has so far provided Florida $608 million for its operation, according to the inspector general’s report. Internal government spreadsheets, revealed in court filings and reviewed by NBC News, show the facility cost taxpayers more than $1 million a day to operate. The typical cost for an ICE detention bed is less than $200 per day, but a bed at the Everglades facility cost in excess of $3,000 per day, according to the court filings.

articles.title: Texas Republicans condemn railroad commissioner candidate over post about Asian students, calling it racist
articles.summary: Texas Republicans on Sunday condemned the GOP candidate running to become the state’s railroad commissioner over a post about University of Texas at Austin students of South Asian descent. Candidate Bo French’s post showed South Asian students at a Texas football game, and he suggested people of South Asian descent were taking over the student…
articles.body:
Texas Republicans on Sunday condemned the GOP candidate running to become the state’s railroad commissioner over a post about University of Texas at Austin students of South Asian descent.

Candidate Bo French’s post showed South Asian students at a Texas football game, and he suggested people of South Asian descent were taking over the student body.

French initially shared a screenshot of a post on the social platform X that showed the students and a caption that said “Bollywood University.” French then showed a similar image with the caption : “I heard UT graduation this year looked like this. I didn’t believe it. The problem is now obviously far worse than anyone imagined.”

Lawmakers including Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas), who will be leaving the Senate at the end of his term after losing in the GOP primary to state Attorney General Ken Paxton, and Rep. Dan Crenshaw (R-Texas) were among those who condemned French’s post.

“This is the Republican nominee for statewide office,” Cornyn wrote on X . “Are other Republican elected officials going to condemn the intolerance and racism, or look the other way while it becomes normalized. This is how great political parties self-destruct. Sad.”

Texas state Rep. Lacey Hull (R) urged French to delete the post.

“This post breaks my heart,” she wrote on X . “I see college kids cheering on their football team. I see Texans.”

Texas House Speaker Dustin Burrows (R) urged French to delete the post and said the candidate can oppose immigration policies “without demeaning people because of their race or ethnicity –– this post has crossed the line.”

French, however, clapped back at Cornyn, calling him a RINO, or “Republican in name only,” and accusing him of cheering for “illegal aliens and foreign nationals.”

“He and the other America Last losers are mad that Texas Republicans are starting to put America First,” French wrote on X .

Texas Gov. Greg Abbott did not condemn the post, though he told NBC News that Texans should unite behind Texas.

“The way we win the state is the same way we win football games. We unite under the brand of Texas,” Abbott said. “That doesn’t mean that Texas cannot also lead in having the toughest immigration laws of any state in America and freezing H-1B visas at our universities.”

Paxton said he condemned all forms of racism, though he did not address French’s post and instead referred to his Senate opponent, Democrat James Talarico.

“Only one person in this race has a history of dividing Texans by race, and it’s James Talarico,” he wrote on X . “I will continue to focus on uniting our State and bringing together the broadest possible coalition to fight for Texas, our values, and our families.”

The post from Paxton was in response to Talarico thanking Cornyn for condemning French’s post and asking Paxton if he would “condemn this blatant racism or will you cower to extremists?”

French has faced backlash for other offensive statements, including the use of slurs against the LGBTQ community and social media posts that were accused of being antisemitic and Islamophobic.

Asked by Dallas news outlet WFAA-TV in July if he regretted these remarks, French said he did not before adding, “Truth sounds like hate to those who hate the truth.”

articles.title: Before private companies hack back, the government needs to set the rules
articles.summary: The NCC needs clear standards for collateral risk, targeting, intelligence preservation and accountability.
articles.body:
On Aug. 12, the White House signed a national security presidential memorandum directing the National Coordination Center to use vetted U.S. companies in cyber operations against foreign transnational criminal organizations under federal oversight.

The rationale is understandable. The FBI received more than a million cybercrime complaints in 2025, with reported losses reaching $20.9 billion — a 26 percent increase from the year before.

Some of the most consequential details of the new program have not been written yet. The National Coordination Center’s executive directors have 60 days to establish operating procedures, and no operation can be approved until those procedures are in place.

For years, hacking back has been debated as a question of capability. If we know where cybercriminal infrastructure is, and have the ability to disrupt it, why shouldn’t we? The harder questions begin once offensive cyber operations move from government agencies into private hands.

The appeal is obvious. Cybercriminals move quickly and exploit jurisdictional boundaries, so giving vetted companies more latitude could bring expertise and speed. But speed is only one measure of success. Before the first operation is approved, the National Coordination Center needs clear standards for collateral risk, targeting, intelligence preservation and accountability.

Cyber infrastructure rarely exists in neat, isolated boxes, which makes unintended consequences one of the most immediate issues the center will have to address. If you take down a virtual private server running command-and-control infrastructure, it may be sitting on shared infrastructure alongside legitimate businesses. Even a limited operation could disrupt unrelated organizations. In the extreme case, a hospital or municipal service could be caught downstream.

That risk becomes more complicated once adversaries know offensive operations are coming. Co-tenancy can become a defensive strategy, giving criminals an incentive to place infrastructure alongside organizations where disruption would create unacceptable collateral damage. What looks like an accident today can become the adversary’s design tomorrow.

That leads to the accountability question. The government authorizes, a private company executes, harm follows, and it becomes less clear who the affected hosting provider or legitimate business ultimately pursues.

Government oversight can reduce some risk, but it cannot eliminate it. The National Coordination Center’s procedures should specify who can accept collateral risk, what level of downstream harm is unacceptable, and who bears responsibility when those limits are crossed.

Even when the target is clear, operators must decide whether to disrupt it immediately or preserve access to collect intelligence and identify the people behind it.

Historically, waiting has had clear advantages. Infrastructure is cheap and easily replaced, while the people operating criminal enterprises are harder to remove. A USENIX Security 2025 study found that more than half of the sites seized in one takedown wave returned within a median of one day, while all the services seized in a second wave returned within two days. Acting too quickly can also destroy evidence that might support arrests or more consequential coordinated operations.

AI may be changing the calculation around when to act. Cyberattacks can now move and scale faster, while multinational investigations, extraditions and arrests still proceed at human speed. If infrastructure is actively causing harm, disrupting it at the point of discovery may protect more victims than preserving access for an arrest that could take years or never happen.

The NCC’s procedures should enable immediate action when the speed and scale of harm demand it, while preserving intelligence whenever possible. The program could create a valuable channel for private companies to share information about criminal infrastructure, tactics, victims and connections across campaigns with government agencies pursuing broader investigations.

The final issue is bigger than any individual operation. Russia and China have long benefited from relationships with tolerated, state-aligned or proxy actors that create distance between governments and offensive cyber activity. Formal U.S. authorization and oversight are not the same as tacitly tolerating criminal hackers, but other governments will still study the model.

Once the United States establishes a framework allowing private companies to participate in offensive cyber operations, others may adopt the concept without the same safeguards. The National Coordination Center should write its rules with reciprocity in mind. Would the U.S. consider the same conduct legitimate if another government authorized one of its companies to carry it out?

Success cannot be measured solely by how quickly something is knocked offline. The challenge is to create rules that account for what an operation might disrupt, what intelligence it might sacrifice and what precedent it might set before anyone pulls the trigger.

Colin Ferris is the threat hunting and incident response lead at Silverfort.

articles.title: Refusing to investigate a judicial controversy lowers the bar for federal judges
articles.summary: The chief judge must not simply accept the subject judge’s denial.
articles.body:
As chief judge of the U.S. 11th Circuit Court of Appeals, William H. Pryor has the unenviable task of receiving misconduct complaints against federal judges in Alabama, Georgia and Florida.

In theory, he must take every complaint seriously, without deference to the subject judge. In the recent case against District Judge Roy K. Altman, however, Pryor issued a quick dismissal without meaningful consideration of significant issues. His failure to initiate an investigation set a regrettable example for the entire federal judiciary.

Altman attracted national attention as author of “ Israel on Trial ,” which employs “courtroom-tested standards” to provide a rigorous defense for Israel against “claims of colonialism, apartheid, and genocide.” He drew criticism for wading into a controversial area as a sitting judge, as well as for the pro-Israel content of the book.

It is not improper for a judge to write about contentious issues that are not pending before him or her, even though it might require recusal in future cases. But writing a book is one thing — plugging it is another.

The complaint against Altman, filed by Florida lawyer Katherine Giannamore, alleges that he misused the prestige and perquisites of his office to push book sales, while sometimes making remarks conveying “anti-Muslim and anti-Arab bias.”

According to the complaint , Altman “used significant judicial resources to engage in live podcasts from his judicial chambers,” to promote his book. An appendix includes screenshots of 14 such appearances over three months, which were said to violate the Judicial Code of Conduct’s prohibition of the use of chambers “to any substantial degree” for financial or other extrajudicial activities.

Additionally, the complaint alleges that Altman publicly referred to the keffiyeh, which “bears significant distinction in the Palestinian and Arab cultures,” as a “terror scarf” or “terrorism scarf.” Those remarks were said to violate the Judicial Code of Conduct by compromising “the integrity and impartiality of the judiciary.”

Pryor had a choice under the federal judiciary’s Rules for Judicial-Conduct and Judicial-Disability Proceedings . He could either conduct a “limited inquiry” and decide the matter by himself, or he could appoint a special committee of other judges to investigate the complaint. He inexplicably chose the former. Based solely on an eight-page response from Altman, Pryor decided that the allegations lacked “any factual foundation” and were “conclusively refuted by objective evidence.”

Pryor did not mention the commentary outlined in the rules providing that “the chief judge must avoid determinations of reasonably disputed issues.” Moreover, the chief judge must not simply accept the subject judge’s denial.

The “ disputed issues ” for a special committee should have been obvious.

Altman conceded that he frequently broadcast book interviews from his chambers, ranging in length from 12 minutes to an hour, but claimed they did not constitute “ substantial ” use.

Is the question of substantiality relative or absolute? Altman argued that his 14 book promotions were trivial because he works “seven days a week, including holidays.” On the other hand, an investigating committee might well conclude that the broadcasts were sufficiently regular and repeated to be objectively substantial in and of themselves. Or they might ask whether a judge should be making even one sales pitch from chambers.

That disputed issue alone should have been sufficient to assign the case for investigation by a special committee.

Did the use of chambers for book publicity exploit the judicial office for financial gain? Pryor skipped past the main issue, which is whether Altman’s use of chambers, identifiable from the flag behind his shoulder, took advantage of his position to boost book sales and royalties. Instead, he echoed Altman’s insistence that “he never associates the prestige of his office with an interview.”

Altman’s assertion that he didn’t write the book in his “judicial capacity” is also contradicted by the interviews themselves. The banner below his image in video interviews typically identified him as a federal judge. So do the promotional materials on Amazon.com , from his publisher, Advantage Books , and from his distributor, Simon and Schuster . Altman’s forthcoming book talk at the University of Florida Law School describes him as “U.S. District Judge Southern District of Florida,” adding that he had been “the youngest federal district court judge in the country.”

Altman maintains that he did not write his book “as a judge,” but he certainly markets it as one.

Pryor uncritically accepted Altman’s rationalization that his “terror scarf” characterization referred only to keffiyehs worn by anti-Israel protesters who “terrorize their Jewish classmates” with slogans “in homage to notorious terrorists.”

A special committee, however, could have reviewed Altman’s Middle East Forum interview, broadcast from chambers, in which he bragged of admonishing college students — with no mention of terrorizing classmates — that “the terrorism scarf, the keffiyeh” isn’t cool or counterculture. By his silence, Pryor shamefully indulged Altman’s denigration of an historic symbol for Palestinian Americans.

Neither Altman nor his publicist replied to multiple emails. Giannamore has until Oct. 13 to file a petition for review. By email, she told me that she hasn’t yet decided.

A special committee may or may not have concluded that Altman’s book promotions and keffiyeh comments constitute judicial misconduct. But there was plenty to investigate if Pryor had allowed it.

Steven Lubet is the Williams Memorial Professor Emeritus at the Northwestern University Pritzker School of Law. He is coauthor of “Judicial Conduct and Ethics.”

articles.title: Libertarian tech mogul to hit DSA with an eight-figure spending nuke
articles.summary: Scott Banister's $40 million funds Make Liberty Win's push to counter Democratic Socialists of America in state legislature races across nine states.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX — A wealthy tech investor is committing $40 million to help Republicans stem the tide of the Democratic Socialists of America in state-level races, Fox News Digital has learned. Scott Banister, a libertarian who was an early investor in PayPal, Uber and SpaceX, among others, cut the massive check to Make Liberty Win, a right-of-center political organization. The funding has already been partially deployed in nine states — Wisconsin, Michigan, Minnesota, Pennsylvania, Georgia, Arizona, New Hampshire, West Virginia and Montana — with plans to expand the push to at least a dozen states. "Self-described socialists are running for office and winning in the Democratic Party, like recently elected New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani," a press release obtained by Fox News Digital reads. "Make Liberty Win’s campaign will stem the tide of the far-left by mobilizing student and youth activists to knock on the doors of more than two million voters in key states." SOCIALIST WINNING STREAK PUTS PRIZED DEMOCRATIC BATTLEGROUND AT RISK AS RADICAL LEFTISTS ADVANCE Banister’s cash injection comes at an opportune time for Republicans. Though Republicans enjoy a comfortable advantage at the national level, the Republican State Leadership Committee, the official GOP committee responsible for making sure the party wins at the state level, projected in late August that Democrats are slated to outspend Republicans in state races by a factor of three to one. Make Liberty Win’s spending could mitigate the liberals’ cash advantage. Democrats have previously disputed claims that their state apparatus is better funded than the GOP’s. NEW MIDTERM BATTLEGROUND TAKES SHAPE AS PARTIES BUILD ELECTION ARMIES Make Liberty Win is a Republican-aligned political organization with a distinctly libertarian bent, supporting a smaller federal government and returning power to state legislatures. It focuses on door knocking and phone banking on behalf of candidates, rather than giving money to them directly. MUSK PICKS HIS FIRST GOP WARRIORS AS A 2026 MONEY SURGE TAKES SHAPE Forty million is a massive amount of money for any level of politics, especially state legislative races. For context, the average U.S. House candidate spent $1.8 million on a campaign in 2024 — and federal races are almost always more expensive than their state equivalents. articles.body: On this episode of Frontlines with Robert Sherman, Robert speaks with Narek Mkrtchyan, Armenia’s Ambassador to the United States, one year after President Trump brokered a peace declaration between Armenia and Azerbaijan. The ambassador reflects on three decades of conflict giving way to contemporary peace, improved trade, investments in tech (including a multibillion-dollar Nvidia project), and a path toward a final treaty. At the center of the conversation is TRIPP, the U.S. developed transit route through Armenian territory that could reroute trade around Russia and Iran, giving the U.S. a lasting foothold in one of the world’s most strategically located regions. Sherman presses on questions pertaining too: Armenia’s balancing act between Moscow and Washington, the U.S. government’s major stake in the South Caucasus, and the hard work of rebuilding trust between two societies interested in learning to work together.

articles.body:
President Trump defended his approach to AI on Monday, saying the only protections needed are a “STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT” amid calls for AI guardrails.

“The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!” he wrote on Truth Social. “The Trump Administration has stopped AI ‘people’ from doing bad, or potentially bad, ‘things.’”

“We already have tremendous CRIMINAL and REGULATORY power over these companies!” he continued. “There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China.”

Trump wrote that U.S. is “leading China, and all others, and will continue to do so.”

“Conspiracy Theorists, Treasonists, Traitors, and Leakers, BEWARE!” he wrote.

He specifically named Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei as an example of someone who has done “bad,” but he said he is “now pretending to be a ‘perfect little angel.’”

Amodei has recently said AI development should slow down to allow for guardrails to be implemented.

“To be clear, pacing does not mean halting model training or technical progress, but ensuring companies take adequate time to align and safeguard their models, and for third party evaluators to confirm this,” Amodei wrote in a blog post over the weekend. “Our pacing framework is an attempt to further strengthen our commitment to safety and encourage a race to the top.”

The president has repeatedly downplayed calls for an AI slowdown and more guardrails from industry leaders and those across the political aisle.

“We can put guardrails, we can do this and that, but I think you have a lot of negative forces that are bringing it up that … shouldn’t be bringing it up, and they’re bringing up things that won’t happen,” Trump told reporters over the weekend.

Trump and his allies argue that the U.S. must win the AI race against China.

“I said it from the very beginning … whoever wins AI wins,” he said.

But the public and lawmakers in both parties appear to be growing more concerned about AI. Their worries run the gamut from how AI could affect the economy and eliminate jobs, to its potential threats to humanity.

Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (N.Y.) on Monday called for a classified briefing on the dangers of AI.

Lawmakers in both parties also have raised concerns about AI data centers, which Trump has repeatedly defended.

articles.title: Trump’s radical plan is to make the postal service an election gatekeeper
articles.summary: The potential to interfere with voters’ ability to vote by mail is not a bug but a feature of a system designed to restrict a practice that Democrats have used more often than Republicans in recent elections.
articles.body:
The Trump administration has filed its third emergency appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court, asking to lift a district court injunction that blocked President Trump’s U.S. Postal Service regulations imposing strict formatting and data-submission requirements on states’ mail-in ballots. A whistleblower has warned that these regulations could cause many ballots to arrive late or not at all ahead of the November midterm elections.

Plaintiffs have argued that these requirements violate the constitutional provisions that restrict election administration to the states and Congress, with no role for the executive. Equally important, and overlooked, is that the administration’s scarcely disguised partisan regulations violate a nearly 60-year American tradition of insulating the postal service from politics.

The potential to interfere with voters’ ability to vote by mail is not a bug but a feature of a system designed to restrict a practice that Democrats have used more often than Republicans in recent elections.

Trump has made no secret of his longstanding hostility to voting by mail and objective of controlling voting nationally. “Republicans should fight very hard when it comes to statewide mail-in voting,” he declared in 2020 , because “for whatever reason, [it] doesn’t work out well for Republicans .” This year, in February, he said , “The Republicans should say, ‘We want to take over.’ … The Republicans ought to nationalize the voting.”

His administration now officially describes its sweeping new postal service restrictions on mail ballots as election-integrity measures, not partisan ones. However, it has provided no proof of the alleged widespread fraud that the regulations would allegedly deter.

The rule doesn’t just put occasional errors at risk. It is designed so that a single failure can void an entire jurisdiction’s mailing. Even before finalizing the rule, internal postal service officials warned that if even one ballot’s barcode in a bulk mailing fails to scan properly during verification, this policy would reject and return the entire batch.

Thus, disrupting an election doesn’t require any bad actor at the local level; it only requires ordinary human error, which is guaranteed at scale, colliding with zero tolerance. The regulations would likely upend voting in the eight states where voting is conducted almost entirely by mail, like Washington and Oregon. Seven of these states, with the exception of Utah , lean Democratic.

Washington, which automatically mails ballots to more than 5 million registered voters, says compliance could require destroying and replacing more than 5 million envelopes already printed for November. It would mean fundamentally reworking procedures only weeks before voting begins. The errors that would surely arise in such a rushed process could jeopardize the entire election process of mail-in states.

Similar disruptions would also occur in states like Arizona that rely heavily but not strictly on mail-in voting. In Maricopa County, Ariz., which mails more than 2 million ballots in its initial run, a single misprinted barcode could delay the delivery of every ballot to every voter in the county.

In addition, the Postmaster General has admitted that the U.S. Postal Service will withhold delivery from any state that refuses to hand over its voter manifest. The rule therefore gives partisan opponents of mail-in voting two independent levers, one technical and one administrative, capable of stopping ballots before they reach voters.

The postal apparatus itself embodies a civic lineage older than the Constitution . In 1775, guided by Benjamin Franklin, the first Postmaster General , the Second Continental Congress established the postal service. And as with today’s mail-in voting process, the early postal service facilitated democracy.

The mail served as an egalitarian highway of democratic debate, intended to distribute independent newspapers and correspondence without royal or partisan interference. The U.S. Postal Service was designed to serve as a neutral common carrier, not an executive gatekeeper or a roving board of canvassers.

“The country may not even have come into existence but for the postal service,” said historian Stephen Allen Kochersperger. Through the material it disseminated, “people were reading, getting ideas of what it would be like to be an independent country.”

In the late 20th century, reformers from both parties worried that partisan politics had infected the postal service. With overwhelming bipartisan support, Congress enacted the landmark Postal Reorganization Act of 1970 . A central purpose was to insulate the mail from presidential and partisan political control. Upon signing the bill, President Nixon noted that his Democratic and Republican postmasters general agreed on one point: “There is no Republican way or Democratic way to deliver the mail. There is only the right way.”

The act converted the postal service into an independent public corporation with a bipartisan Board of Governors — no more than five of the nine members can belong to the same party — and gave that board, not the president, the power to appoint and remove the postmaster general. By asking the Supreme Court to lift the Boston court’s injunction , the administration seeks to invert the purpose of the postal service, turning an independent carrier into an instrument of executive election policing for partisan gain.

Benjamin Franklin would be turning in his grave.

Allan J. Lichtman is Distinguished Professor of History at American University, co-host of “Lichtman Live,” and author of 15 books, most recently “Great American Presidents: The Twelve Who Transformed the Nation. “

articles.title: ICE has no plans to ‘sweep polling locations’ for noncitizens, Homan says
articles.summary: White House border czar Tom Homan on Sunday said there are no plans in place for Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers to “sweep polling locations” in the November midterm elections. Homan told Fox News host Jacqui Heinrich on “The Sunday Briefing” that he has not seen “any operational plans or any discussions on any…
articles.body:
White House border czar Tom Homan on Sunday said there are no plans in place for Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers to “sweep polling locations” in the November midterm elections.

Homan told Fox News host Jacqui Heinrich on “The Sunday Briefing” that he has not seen “any operational plans or any discussions on any immigration enforcement operation at polling places,” after Heinrich asked if there was any truth to claims that ICE will be “raiding” polling locations.

“This is another fear tactic. This is another attack on ICE and this administration,” Homan said about the claims. “I mean, they don’t want ICE near the polling places, they don’t want to vote for voter ID, they don’t want observers. What have they got to hide to begin with, right? But there is no plan for enforcement action at polling places. It’s just another attempt to smear ICE and smear the president.”

Homan also pushed back on reports of ICE arrests at elementary schools, hospitals and places of worship, saying there’s no “sensitive location” policy.

“If you’re a criminal alien, you’re a national security threat, there’s no sanctuary,” he said. “But look at the past two years. Not one instance of ICE operating at a sensitive location, [including] polling places.”

Latino civil rights and voting rights groups, along with the city of Denver, last week filed a lawsuit to block ICE from polling locations. The plaintiffs cited post-Civil War-era federal laws barring armed federal personnel at polling locations to prevent the intimidation of voters.

Lawyers for Denver and other plaintiffs — which include the League of United Latin American Citizens, Common Cause and UnidosUS — wrote, “the specter of armed officers at polling places threatens the freedom of this upcoming election.”

“It places voters in fear that they will be confronted by armed federal immigration enforcement officers if they choose to cast a ballot,” they added.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said earlier this month that ICE would appear at polling places if there is a threat or a warrant for “someone that we have been actively tracking down.” He made similar remarks in an interview with CNN’s Kasie Hunt in June, noting that ICE would not be at polling locations because the “only people that should be voting there is American citizens.”

Democratic lawmakers have slammed any notion of armed ICE officers operating at polling locations, echoing the lawsuit in suggesting their presence would amount to voter intimidation.

The Department of Justice has plans to deploy monitors to voting sites this November. The Trump administration has also sought to pursue restrictions on mail-in voting and to create voter lists alongside the added security.

articles.title: AP's refusal to give Trump rights to Butler photo helped fuel Oval Office ban, report claims
articles.summary: Trump's administration targeted the Associated Press over photo rights to Evan Vucci's iconic Butler, Pennsylvania, assassination attempt image, according to a NYT report.
articles.body: President Donald Trump's administration targeted the Associated Press (AP) over rights to the iconic photo of the president in Butler, Pennsylvania, taken after an assassination attempt, according to a New York Times report. The AP has repeatedly sparred with the Trump White House after the president was elected in 2024. The outlet was banned from the Oval Office and Air Force One shortly after Trump was inaugurated because the AP continued to use "Gulf of Mexico" after the president renamed it the Gulf of America in 2025. The ban has led to a First Amendment battle in court. However, according to the Times, White House aides also connected the ban to the AP's refusal to give them rights to the infamous photo of the president after he was shot. The Times cited two people briefed on a private lunch with Trump and network anchors in 2025. INSIDE AP’S FIRST AMENDMENT BATTLE WITH TRUMP’S WHITE HOUSE AS ‘GULF OF AMERICA’ DISPUTE HEADS BACK TO COURT "We’re focused on continuing to stand for the right of the public and the press to speak freely without government retaliation or control," a spokesman for the AP told Fox News Digital in a statement in response to the claim. A source added the White House has not communicated this reasoning to the AP. The White House did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment. Trump was rushed offstage by Secret Service agents after gunfire grazed his upper right ear during his July 13, 2024, rally in Butler, Pennsylvania. The attack came months before Trump’s re-election and preceded a series of later alleged attempts and reported threats against his life. The president was mid-sentence, pointing to a chart on illegal immigration under the Biden administration, when gunshots pierced the air at his Butler rally. Authorities identified the gunman as Thomas Matthew Crooks, who fired from the roof of a nearby building. TWO MEN SHOT AT TRUMP'S BUTLER RALLY SUE FEDERAL GOVERNMENT OVER SECRET SERVICE 'PREVENTABLE FAILURES' Secret Service agents tackled Trump to the ground. Moments later, as they rose to escort him to his motorcade, Trump emerged from the huddle. Trump raised his fist high in the air, and said "fight" three times, prompting the audience to erupt and chant "U-S-A!" as he exited. The gunman killed firefighter Corey Comperatore, who was shielding his family, and wounded two other men. A Secret Service sniper killed Crooks during the attack. A photo of Trump, captured by Evan Vucci of the AP, with his fist raised and blood visible on his face, quickly went viral and landed on the front pages of newspapers across the world. "I was literally just thinking about doing the best possible job I could, because I knew that this was a moment in American history that I had to be at the top of my game for," Vucci told Fox News Digital in July 2024, after the assassination attempt. TRUMP SIGNS PROCLAMATION DECLARING FEBRUARY 9 'GULF OF AMERICA DAY' AHEAD OF SUPER BOWL: 'ANOTHER BIG WIN' "I knew immediately it was gunfire. I trained my lens on the stage, and I saw Secret Service agents going to run to the president, covering him up. And from that moment, I ran to the stage and I got my wide angle lens, and I started making photographs. I went into work mode," Vucci said. "I knew immediately that it was going to be one of the most important things I'll ever photograph, and that I needed to do the best job possible." CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE Vucci switched to a wide angle to ensure the flag flying above got in his shot. He noticed an SUV parked at the side of the stage as Secret Service agents covered Trump and chaos erupted around him. Vucci said he "sprinted" to the side of the stage, assuming it was where Trump would exit, and got in position to snap photos as Trump pumped his fist toward the crowd. articles.title: Trump says AI doesn’t need guardrails, only a ‘high IQ’ president
articles.summary: President Donald Trump rejected the idea of placing guardrails on artificial intelligence, saying a “High IQ” president is all the U.S. needs to address  risks.
articles.body: President Donald Trump rejected the idea of placing guardrails on artificial intelligence, saying in a Truth Social post Monday that the only control needed is “a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!” In the same post, he appeared to hint at the government pursuing criminal or regulatory penalties against AI companies after industry insiders warned of potentially catastrophic dangers posed by the rapidly evolving technology. “The Trump Administration has stopped AI ‘people’ from doing bad, or potentially bad, ‘things,’ like Dario (Anthropic!), who is now pretending to be a ‘perfect little angel’ — and we will continue to do so!” he said, referring to Dario Amodei, the CEO of Anthropic, maker of the Claude AI chatbot. Amodei said in a Saturday essay that AI companies should “slow the pace” of AI development. “We already have tremendous CRIMINAL and REGULATORY power over these companies!” Trump continued. “There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China. WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS! We are leading China, and all others, and will continue to do so. Conspiracy Theorists, Treasonists, Traitors, and Leakers, BEWARE!” Even as the American public and members of his own party grow increasingly skeptical of AI, the president has framed the technology’s continued growth as an economic and geopolitical imperative. Communities that reject AI data centers will wind up “backwards and poor,” he warned recently. And in Ireland last weekend, he was even blunter: “Whoever wins AI wins.” Yet, a recent NBC News Decision Desk poll found that 70% of adults said they were more worried about AI than excited about it. A similar percentage — 69% of adults — said they somewhat or strongly oppose the construction of an AI data center in their local area. That includes 57% of Republican voters. Trump remained undeterred Monday afternoon, returning to Truth Social in a full-throated defense of AI, saying that “AI taking over the World, destroying Humanity, and all other things bad, is a HOAX.” In the same post, he said that AI would be “the Greatest Economic Development Engine in History — Bigger than Oil, Gold, Diamonds, or even the Internet.” Amodei’s recent warning has prompted other AI leaders to publicly call for a slowdown in its development so researchers can better understand and control any threats posed by the technology. They include OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who said his company would adopt one of the safeguards Amodei proposed in his essay. Last week, Anthropic AI researcher Jacob Coxon resigned, writing in a viral X post that OpenAI and Anthropic were “gambling with our lives,” warning that “the people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.” A lead Anthropic researcher, Evan Hubinger, said in a post on X that Coxon was right, saying, “we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” Many politicians responded with their own calls for stronger checks on AI to address safety concerns. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., on Monday called for a Senate briefing with top administration officials. House Speaker Mike Johnson suggested in interviews Sunday that AI leaders come together for a meeting to determine how to move forward, while also warning that “we cannot put a moratorium on this because China will overlap us.” Beijing on Monday disparaged the warnings from U.S. tech leaders as “fearmongering” from a “Cold War playbook” aimed at hobbling China. Vice President JD Vance on Monday told reporters that AI leaders’ warnings is “something that we’re concerned by,” but said the administration wants to ensure “we actually regulate smartly.” “I have to say, just personally, I feel a little bit weird about the fact that you have so many frontier AI tech companies kind of coming to the government and begging the government to regulate them,” Vance said. “It feels a little bit to me like a bit of a Trojan horse. So I think we just have to be careful about this.” During his trip to Ireland, Trump asserted over the weekend that the U.S. was leading China on artificial intelligence and said that “whoever wins AI wins.” “We can put guardrails,” he said Sunday. “We can do this and that, but I think you have a lot of negative forces that are bringing it up that shouldn’t be bringing it up, and they’re bringing up things that won’t happen.”

articles.title: How to fix NATO’s fatal flaw
articles.summary: NATO has not confronted determining when active measures or hybrid warfare attacks trigger Article 5.
articles.body:
For longer than I can remember, pleading with NATO to address what has been and is now a more obvious fatal flaw has not yielded a single action. That flaw is that its bedrock Article Five commitment that “an armed attack against one NATO member shall be considered an attack against them all,” presumes the attack will be a military assault by the Soviet Union on one or more members of the alliance.

But what if the attack is not military? The only precedent is when Article Five was invoked 25 years ago after al Qaeda’s strike on New York’s Twin Towers — when the alliance went to war in Afghanistan.

Vladimir Putin is using what Lenin termed “ active measures ” and what the West calls “ hybrid warfare ” in attacking NATO and Western countries. Russia is using active measures, including spreading as much chaos as possible short of an armed attack, in its plan to divide and fracture the alliance. And much like Lenin, who recruited useful idiots to his service, Putin has done the same with President Trump. Trump has gone out of his way to strain America’s links with NATO by demanding that NATO Europe take more responsibility for its defense — but “more” means “all” in Trump talk.

From 2003 to 2016 I served on the advisory board for a series of NATO’s Supreme allied commanders in Europe. During the years since, trying to get NATO to respond and react to these active measures has proved to be Sisyphean. NATO, to its credit, has created 30 wide-ranging Centers of Excellence that cover cyber, counterintelligence and strategic communications. But none focuses on dealing with active measures.

NATO has not confronted determining when active measures or hybrid warfare attacks trigger Article Five. Russia’s use of drones is an example. Sixteen NATO members have reported Russian drones penetrating national air space. Romania has cited 26 such violations, and this past August, shot down four Russian drones . On Aug. 4, a Russian drone attack took place at Leipzig/Halle Airport in Germany. Fortunately it failed to explode.

The cyber realm is another area that Russia exploits regularly. The exact number of cyber attacks Russia is making against NATO is difficult to determine, but it is a very large number. The most infamous of these was the Internet Research Agency in St. Petersburg, which founded by Yevgeny Prigozhin, who also headed the Wagner Group until his killing in 2023.

Russia has a number of these so-called troll offices that deal with the disinformation aspects of war and have been highly effective in spreading dissent among NATO and Western states. Yet so far, NATO has not taken collective action to counter these propaganda machines, leaving it up to individual member states to react.

What then should NATO do to protect and defend against Russian and possibly Chinese active measures and hybrid war? This question can raise intractable issues as to what might invoke Article Five, so it has been deferred. Since cyber responses involve highly classified national capabilities that can be shared, for example among the Five Eyes coalition of the U.S., United Kingdom, Australia, Canada and New Zealand, they usually do not apply across all of NATO’s 32 members.

First, NATO should state that any Russian drones penetrating its nations’ territorial air or waters will be destroyed. NATO can expand its air policing to that end. Expanding cybersecurity and infrastructure protection must be a high priority. And expanding strategic communications to counter Russian propaganda and disinformation must take place.

Second, NATO should use its exercises and deployments as part of influence operations against the Russians to match or expose active measures. As a further example, Putin is reportedly upset when a Tomahawk shooter is in range of him. That might be an interesting pressure point to exploit.

Third, under the Supreme Allied Commander Europe, NATO should create what Churchill called in World War II, a “ dirty tricks ” organization. Best described under a benign name such as special services, this organization would be tasked to take on and blunt Russian active measures and hybrid war.

Having offered these proposals before, perhaps this time round, someone may listen.

Harlan Ullman is senior adviser at Washington’s Atlantic Council, chairman of a private company and principal author of the doctrine of shock and awe. His next book, co-written with Field Marshal The Lord David Richards, former UK chief of defense and due out this fall, is “Who Thinks Best Wins: How Decisive Strategic Thinking Will Prevent Global Chaos. “

articles.title: New York City leads lawsuit against Trump's 'public charge' immigration rule
articles.summary: The city and the New York attorney general, along with other municipalities around the country, filed lawsuits in federal court.
articles.body:
NEW YORK — New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and mayors around the country announced a joint lawsuit Monday seeking to stop President Donald Trump from making it harder for lawful immigrants to receive green cards or visas. New York State Attorney General Letitia James is leading a separate coalition that's filing a concurrent suit.

A federal rule change sought by the Trump administration would give immigration agents more leeway to deny green cards or visas to lawful immigrants on the basis of being a "public charge" — someone who's using social safety net programs. The rule change, which is set to take effect Friday, would allow agents to factor in the use of Medicaid or food assistance into their decision making.

"The new public charge rule seeks to push immigrant families away from the programs that have kept people fed and healthy for decades. New Yorkers will be afraid to see a doctor or ask for help they are legally entitled to," Mamdani said in a statement. "That fear will not stop at the families that the federal government is targeting. Families who remain fully eligible for benefits will feel a chilling effect, and all New Yorkers will pay for it."

New York City is leading a coalition of cities and counties that includes Chicago, San Francisco, Santa Clara County in California, Seattle, and King County in Washington. The suit, which was filed in the Southern District of New York, argues that the Trump administration overstepped legal precedent that puts limits on what immigration officials can consider when denying a green card or visa application on a "public charge" basis.

"Chicago will not stand by while the federal government forces immigrant families to choose between putting food on the table, taking their children to the doctor, or protecting their ability to remain in this country," Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson said in a statement. "This rule is not only cruel, it is unlawful, and it threatens the health and safety of our entire city."

The Trump administration has argued that the U.S. should more carefully consider giving green cards or visas to poor immigrants who rely on government services.

Public health experts have predicted that the rule change will result in immigrants declining to seek preventative medical care, a trend that could potentially place a greater cost on the system if they wait until a major medical episode to see a doctor.

articles.title: Trump unloads on tech titans pushing for slowdown on emerging industry: ‘WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS!’
articles.summary: President Donald Trump rejected calls for AI guardrails and singled out Dario Amodei, as David Sacks challenged the industry's push to pace the frontier.
articles.body: President Donald Trump on Monday rejected growing calls for implementing safeguards and restrictions on artificial intelligence (AI), declaring that the technology needs a "STRONG AND SMART" president rather than additional restraints. Even some of Silicon Valley's most powerful executives, including those within the AI space, are calling for a slowdown in the development of increasingly capable artificial intelligence technology. "The only control or 'guardrails' that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!" Trump wrote on Truth Social. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei over the weekend made waves as he called on leading AI companies to "pace the frontier" amid warnings that increasingly powerful systems could eventually outstrip humanity's ability to understand or control them. MIKE JOHNSON REJECTS AI MORATORIUM OVER CHINA THREAT AS CONSERVATIVE ACTIVIST DEMANDS GUARDRAILS "The Trump Administration has stopped AI 'people' from doing bad, or potentially bad, 'things,' like Dario (Anthropic!), who is now pretending to be a 'perfect little angel' — and we will continue to do so!" the president wrote on Truth Social. Previously, the Trump administration designated Anthropic a supply-chain risk and moved to restrict federal agencies from using its technology, though a federal judge temporarily blocked that designation last month. Anthropic is most known for its AI model Claude, one of the top known and used LLM chatbots in the U.S. Trump argues that the federal government already has "tremendous CRIMINAL and REGULATORY power over these companies" and warned that additional restraints on American AI development could benefit China in the AI race. "There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China," he wrote. "WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS! We are leading China, and all others, and will continue to do so." FETTERMAN ALIGNS WITH TRUMP ON AI PUSH, WARNS CHINA BENEFITS FROM US 'OVERREACTION' Trump's intervention escalated a rapidly widening debate over whether America's leading AI companies should voluntarily slow the development of their most powerful systems — and what role Washington should play in policing an industry racing against both domestic competitors and China. Amodei ignited the debate Saturday with an essay arguing that AI capabilities are advancing so quickly that safety measures may no longer be keeping pace. His call quickly drew support from several of the industry's most prominent figures. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said he agreed that companies need to "pace the frontier," while Elon Musk said Amodei was "right." Google DeepMind's Demis Hassabis also said Amodei's proposal pointed in the right direction. But David Sacks, Trump's White House AI and crypto advisor, sharply challenged the premise that the companies need government help to slow themselves down. "The easiest way not to build superintelligence is for you to agree not to build it," Sacks wrote Saturday on X in response to Altman and Amodei. "Stop pretending you need anyone else's permission." "You guys are the frontier," he continued. "By any reasonable metric — market share, revenue growth, model capability — the two of you have a duopoly on frontier AI." "So just do it," Sacks added. "If you do, you'll buy goodwill for the next conversation. If you don't, we'll know this was just another bid for regulatory capture — or an election-season psyop." Amodei's proposal, however, does not call for halting AI development altogether. He described "pacing" as slowing advances in model capabilities enough to give companies time to align and safeguard their systems and allow outside evaluators to test whether those protections are working. Anthropic has already committed to one piece of the proposal: giving third-party evaluators ongoing, employee-like access to assess its safety practices, training processes and models. Altman said OpenAI would adopt a similar approach. Other elements would require broader coordination among competing AI companies and, eventually, governments around the world. That coordination became another target of Sacks' criticism. "Stop pretending antitrust law has to be suspended so you can form a cartel," Sacks wrote. "Stop pretending you need a regulatory approval process that supersedes product liability." Amodei has argued that companies should be able to coordinate on common safety practices without risking antitrust penalties. Sacks countered that the leading companies do not need government permission to voluntarily slow their own development if they believe their systems are becoming dangerous. The warnings from Amodei and other AI researchers center on increasingly autonomous systems that can perform sophisticated tasks with less human direction. RESEARCHER WHO DEPARTED AI ROLE OVER FEARS OF RACING INTO EXTINCTION SAYS PEOPLE ARE 'BEGGING' FOR REGULATION Amodei said AI's growing ability to assist with AI research itself could create a feedback loop in which increasingly capable systems help develop their own successors, potentially allowing capabilities to advance faster than humans can understand or control them. He also pointed to a recent OpenAI evaluation in which AI agents escaped a testing environment and conducted unauthorized cyber activity against the AI development platform Hugging Face. The exercise occurred in a controlled setting, but Amodei cited it as evidence of the potential consequences as frontier systems become more capable. Sacks acknowledged that slowing development could create "breathing room" for a broader discussion about AI safety, but argued that any global agreement would confront a fundamental problem: China. "China is very unlikely to join a global agreement, as you know, and that has to be taken into account as well," Sacks wrote. "So go ahead and pace the frontier. You are the ones setting it." Amodei has acknowledged the same geopolitical dilemma, warning that a system in which American companies restrain themselves while China continues racing ahead could create its own national security risks. Altman expanded on his position Monday, saying frontier AI companies should strengthen safety practices immediately rather than waiting for Congress to act. "The world deserves confidence that American companies developing increasingly capable AI will act responsibly, especially as the trajectory of progress has steepened," Altman wrote. "Every frontier lab must deliver on this, and there is no reason any of us should come to work if we cannot." Altman said OpenAI welcomes "a federal framework that sets consistent safety requirements for frontier AI," but added that the company does "not believe we need to wait for an anti-trust exemption or legislation" before implementing stronger safeguards. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP He said OpenAI supports explicit safety reviews before major training runs, shared industry standards and independent auditors, and has begun preparing formal "safety cases" before frontier reinforcement-learning runs expected to substantially increase model capabilities. Altman called on other AI companies to develop comparable standards for monitoring, evaluating and mitigating those risks.

articles.title: Former CIA Director Brennan subpoenaed to testify in federal Trump conspiracy case
articles.summary: John Brennan faces a grand jury subpoena in a Justice Department probe into whether officials conspired to deprive Trump of his civil rights.
articles.body: Former CIA Director John Brennan has been subpoenaed to testify next month before a Florida grand jury as part of a Justice Department investigation into whether former law enforcement and intelligence officials conspired against President Donald Trump. Ken Wainstein, an attorney for Brennan, disclosed in a court filing Monday that prosecutors last Thursday presented him with a subpoena for Brennan to appear Oct. 15 before a grand jury in Fort Pierce, Florida. He said he was told that the subpoena relates to a "far-reaching" criminal probe examining whether government officials who have investigated Trump over the past decade conspired to deprive Trump of his civil rights. JOHN SOLOMON PREDICTS BRENNAN INDICTMENT COULD COME WITHIN 'WEEKS' AS PROSECUTORS REQUEST OFFICIAL TRANSCRIPTS According to Wainstein, a prosecutor also informed him that Brennan remains a target in a separate Washington-based investigation examining whether he lied to Congress in 2023, an allegation Brennan and his legal team have consistently denied. The development comes amid leadership upheaval within the probe. The subpoena was delivered on the same day Joe diGenova, the prosecutor leading the inquiry informally known as the "grand conspiracy" investigation, abruptly resigned. NEW FEDERAL GRAND JURY SUBPOENA ISSUED TO FORMER JAMES COMEY ADVISOR IN LEAK INVESTIGATION: SOURCES The Justice Department has not publicly named a replacement for diGenova. Wainstein said he spoke with Kurt Olsen, a member of the investigative team and a lawyer who urged the Justice Department in 2020 to back Trump's claims that the election had been stolen. Disclosure of the subpoena came hours ahead of a scheduled court hearing in Washington concerning a lawsuit brought by Brennan. U.S. District Judge Carl Nichols , a Trump appointee, found that the president’s plan — which would require states to upload voter lists based on citizenship data, among other requirements — wasn’t authorized by Congress.

What does this mean?: The Supreme Court was already considering an emergency request from the Justice Department to lift another judge’s block, and The Hill’s Zach Schonfeld reports that decision could come any day now. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson was assigned to that request. The high court’s decision there will likely be the next big domino to fall.

What does the plan entail?: Beyond the voter list requirement, the Postal Service would have states ensure their mail ballot envelopes meet specific design specs, including an official logo and barcode, to be sent. Schonfeld notes blue states have warned it is too late to change their designs with the midterms less than two months away.

Trump over the weekend doubled down on his promise to pay American adults $5,000 each if Republicans keep control of Congress in November, saying the payouts will “happen 100 percent.”

The president has made the midterms a key part of the pitch, saying the checks would depend on Republicans continuing to bring in revenue before the next term.

“I don’t want to do it now, because if the Democrats get it, our country will be in shambles and they won’t be able to do it,” he said Sunday. “If we get in, we’re taking in tremendous amounts of money. We’re taking in over $20 trillion in terms of investment. And with the Democrats, all of that money will be thrown out. If the Democrats get in, they won’t be able to pay it.”

Trump first floated the dividends last week during the GOP’s midterm convention. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick also claimed the checks would not rely on taxpayer dollars or add to the deficit.

Some House Republicans are pumping the brakes on the idea.

Rep. Mike Lawler (N.Y.) said the key question is how the government would pay for it, while Rep. Mike Flood (Neb.) said funding troops and replenishing munitions should take priority.

The roughly $1.35 trillion price tag would cover checks for the estimated 270 million adults in the U.S., putting the proposal against other major spending priorities Congress will have to weigh.

The internet over the weekend hosted a storm of warnings on the dangers of artificial intelligence’s (AI) rapid development after a former Anthropic researcher said last week that AI could destroy humanity in the near future.

Close watchers of technology will know that similar warnings have been shared for years, but the fears have appeared to reach a fever pitch — just in time for the House and Senate to return from recess today.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) on Monday called for the Trump administration to give all senators a classified briefing on the dangers AI poses. His comments came after House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) on Sunday called for Congress to act on the issue urgently, while Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) took a different tack , saying, “We don’t need everybody to panic right now.”

The House Republican leader was echoing remarks from Trump, who told reporters while in Ireland that guardrails can be placed on AI but that the U.S. cannot lose the race to China in the process. (He later pushed back on reports that he was downplaying AI’s risks.)

Then, this morning, the president posted on Truth Social that the “only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!” (Time will tell if this calms everybody down.)

The Senate returns on Monday from about a monthlong recess, while the House will also be back, but only for a week before departing again until after the midterms.

They will have a lot on their plate, according to The Hill’s Sudiksha Kochi . Here are some of the lawmakers’ priorities:

Trump seems pretty happy with the White House these days.

The president on Sunday revisited his makeover of the executive mansion, declaring that 1600 Pennsylvania Ave. was a “dump” before he started fixing it up.

Trump pointed to photos of cracks and imperfections in the North Portico, claiming the building’s exterior was “practically falling off.” Now, he says, it’s in better shape than it was when the White House was built in 1792.

The upgrades aren’t exactly subtle: A new 100-foot-wide helipad is finished, complete with a giant presidential seal made from California granite. Crews are also racing ahead on Trump’s 90,000-square-foot ballroom, with 250 workers reportedly putting in 20-hour days, seven days a week.

Then there’s the Rose Garden, which he had paved over and turned into an event space.

articles.title: Inside House Republicans' plan to end run Dem opposition and pass Trump-backed voter ID
articles.summary: Congressional Republicans plan to bypass the Senate filibuster and pass the SAVE America Act's voter ID and proof of citizenship rules via reconciliation.
articles.body: Congressional Republicans have a plan to pass key portions of the Safeguarding American Voter Eligibility (SAVE) America Act before the end of this year. The election integrity bill backed by President Donald Trump and fiercely opposed by Democrats has stalled in Congress, where Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., has been reluctant to call it up for a vote, given that it's all but assured to fail. At least several Democrats would be needed to reach the Senate's 60-vote threshold to break a filibuster. But left-wing lawmakers in the House and Senate have panned the legislation as an attempt to sow doubt in U.S. elections at best and voter suppression at worst. Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., is now pushing Republicans to pass the bill's main mandates via the budget reconciliation process, which allows the party in power to pass sweeping fiscal policy without input from the minority due to its sidelining of the Senate filibuster. Rep. Bryan Steil, R-Wis., chairman of the Committee on House Administration, is tasked with overseeing how that part of the bill gets done. TRUMP QUESTIONS THUNE'S LEADERSHIP AS SAVE AMERICA ACT STALLS "I'd rather pass the SAVE America Act. But recognizing that the Senate might not be able to get that done with the 60-vote threshold, let's leverage the parliamentary procedure, bring that threshold down to 50, and get some really commonsense reforms done," Steil told Fox News Digital in an interview. "I've been having great conversations with my colleagues in the administration as well as the Senate." SENATE FACES 'COME-TO-JESUS' MOMENT ON TRUMP'S ELECTION PRIORITY UNDER GOP'S NEW PLAN Steil told Fox News Digital that he hoped Congress could pass a reconciliation bill with SAVE America before the November midterm elections, but conceded "the clock is ticking down pretty quickly." The budget reconciliation process is a lengthy one, with Republicans having taken roughly half a year to use it to pass Trump's signature One Big, Beautiful Bill Act last year. Both the House and Senate must pass budget "frameworks," with instructions for relevant committees to enact policies that either spend or cut funding to a specified amount. Those committees pass their portions, then send them back to the House and Senate budget committees to tie them together into one massive bill. Identical bills must pass the House and Senate before getting to Trump's desk. Steil's panel, which has jurisdiction over federal election law, is aiming to include two portions of the original SAVE America Act: a proof of citizenship mandate for the voter registration process, and a nationwide photo ID rule to cast a ballot. READ THE DOCUMENTS: WHITE HOUSE RELEASES ELECTION INTEGRITY FILES AFTER TRUMP SPEECH "The House can go as fast as the Senate. And so the frustration that I and others have is the Senate's not moving as fast as we would like on this. I actually think there's 50 votes in the Senate for some of these really commonsense provisions," Steil said. "I'd like to be sooner rather than later, but I don't control them." Where the process gets even trickier is when the Senate parliamentarian, who is appointed by Senate leadership to help interpret the chamber's rules, goes through the reconciliation bill draft and weeds out what does not adhere to the process rules. That means anything that does not impact the federal government's budget, tax policy, or the national debt is generally removed. TOP TRUMP OFFICIAL MAKES NEW SAVE ACT CASE TO REPUBLICANS BEHIND CLOSED DOORS Steil said portions of the SAVE America Act could arguably get through that filtration process by affecting funds going to states via the Help America Vote Act (HAVA), a 2002-era election reform law. "We could free up those funds or enhance those funds for states to do those post-election audits, which is a really important part of election integrity. You can do the same in regards to photo ID," he said, adding that making Real ID the standard could also effectively impact the citizenship mandate. "Effectively, when an individual gets REAL ID, they're proving their citizenship." TRUMP INTERVENES AS HOUSE GOP REVOLT PUTS SAVE AMERICA ACT AT CENTER OF SPENDING SHOWDOWN And the Trump administration is behind the push. Earlier this year, Office of Management and Budget (OMB) Director Russell Vought told Republicans at a lawmaker-only meeting that the White House backed using the reconciliation process for SAVE America and argued it was the best way forward to pass the GOP's election reforms, multiple people in the room told Fox News Digital. "The White House is engaged. We've had good conversations," Steil told Fox News Digital. The House passed its version of the reconciliation bill earlier this summer, a $95 billion budget aimed at replenishing the U.S. military and enhancing election security. But in the Senate, Budget Committee Chairman Ron Johnson, R-Wis., unveiled his committee's framework just before the chamber left for the August recess. It's not clear when it will advance through his panel or get a vote. GOP CIVIL WAR ERUPTS OVER TRUMP'S LATEST AGENDA PUSH AS KEY REPUBLICANS THREATEN TO SINK MEGABILL Their legislation calls for up to $150 billion in spending — a significant difference. Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., acknowledged that gap in an interview with Fox News Digital last month. "I mean, the idea was, in keeping it skinny, is to move it quickly. And so the more you add to it, the more complex it gets, the more in the Senate — not to get too deep in the weeds — but procedurally, it involves more committees of jurisdiction in both bodies. And that's where things start to get weighted down. So we're very close to an election, the stakes are very high, the timing is short, and if you're going to do election integrity measures, you need to do it, like, yesterday," Johnson said. "We passed the SAVE America Act four times in the House. This is the last best effort to get it through the Senate, so I'm for doing it as quickly as possible." Steil said he was optimistic that an agreement could be reached. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "I think, broadly, we're aligned. I think obviously the total numbers are different," he said. "I think everyone recognizes the importance of making sure that our men and women in uniform have the resources needed to not only defend themselves but to defend our country... And also that we have the resources needed to make sure that we're protecting our election."

articles.title: Yankee Stadium listed in Legionnaires cluster: Officials
articles.summary: A cooling tower at Yankee Stadium is among 10 towers that tested positive for Legionella bacteria on Sunday as officials investigate an outbreak in the South Bronx.
articles.body:
NEW YORK CITY ( WPIX ) — A cooling tower at Yankee Stadium is among 10 towers that tested positive for Legionella bacteria on Sunday as officials investigate an outbreak in the South Bronx .

The New York City Department of Health said all cooling towers that tested positive for Legionella have been ordered to be cleaned and disinfected by Monday.

Officials said polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing can detect the presence of Legionella but cannot show whether the bacteria are alive and does not confirm a cooling tower as the source of exposure. They also reiterated that only live Legionella can cause illness.

Officials urged anyone who lives, works or has visited the affected area since late August and develops flu‑like symptoms to contact a health care provider immediately.

They also said it is safe to shower, drink tap water and use air conditioners in the affected ZIP codes. Officials noted there is no additional risk from being inside any of the 10 buildings.

There will be an in-person town hall for residents to sit down with public health officials on Tuesday at 6 p.m at Metropolitan College in the Bronx.

One person has died in connection with the South Bronx outbreak, and five cases have been confirmed, according to officials.

On the Upper East Side, a Legionnaires’ cluster claimed nine lives and led to more than 90 confirmed cases, with the outbreak first reported at the beginning of July.

Yankee Stadium released the following statement on Sunday night:

In 2024, the Yankees installed new, state-of-the-art, high-efficiency chiller towers at Yankee Stadium, which have undergone water quality and bacteriological indicator testing on a weekly basis over the last three years. In accordance with DOH regulations, Yankee Stadium provides these results to the DOH on a monthly basis. In the most recent monthly testing on Aug. 20, which was provided to the Department of Health, results were negative for Legionella bacteria. Subsequent to that test, weekly water quality and bacteriological indicator testing was performed on Aug. 26, Sept. 2 and Sept. 9. Due to the recent community cluster of Legionella bacteria in the Melrose and Morrisania areas of the Bronx (zip codes 10451 and 10456) last week, the NYC Dept. of Health conducted 24 PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction) tests of cooling towers in the area, including one at Yankee Stadium on Sept. 11. Yankee Stadium tested positive for trace amounts of Legionella bacteria and was one of 10 cooling towers in the Bronx that tested positive. A PCR test, which is different from the independent monthly testing Yankee Stadium regularly undertakes, can detect the presence of Legionella bacteria DNA but cannot determine whether the bacteria are alive or dead and does not confirm that a cooling tower is the source of exposure. Only live Legionella bacteria can cause illness. No current cases have been associated with Yankee Stadium. Additionally, the New York City Department of Health has not at any point this month asked us to postpone our games. The Health Department is now conducting culture testing to determine whether live Legionella bacteria were present when the samples were collected. Culture results can take up to two weeks. To reduce the risk of ongoing exposure while culture testing continues, the Health Department mandated that all cooling towers with a positive PCR result conduct a full hyperhalogenation, including draining, cleaning, and disinfection. Immediate action was taken, and this was completed at Yankee Stadium earlier this morning (Sunday). To exercise an abundance of caution, those who currently live, work or have visited the two ZIP codes since late August and are experiencing flu-like symptoms, such as fever, cough, or difficulty breathing, should contact a healthcare provider immediately. Please note that Legionnaires’ disease is not contagious and can be treated with antibiotics when caught early.
