articles.title: Far-left attack backfires spectacularly as radical online personality whines after attacking female Trump aide
articles.summary: Aaron Rupar faces White House backlash after attacking a female press wrangler in a C-SPAN clip from President Trump's Ireland departure.
articles.body: A self-styled leftist journalist who chronicles President Donald Trump's moves online is crying foul after he made another attack on a young female Trump staffer, part of a pattern he's been engaged in for weeks. "another [sic] blonde Trump flunkie starts literally shoving photographers away from Trump," Aaron Rupar posted on his X account on Sunday afternoon, attaching a clip from C-SPAN showing Trump greeting family members next to Air Force 1 as he prepared to board the plane leaving Ireland. The clip shows Ellie Acra, a White House press wrangler, sternly directing the media to exit the area underneath the wing of the plane, using the often-employed phrase: "Thank you, press." White House press wranglers are the grunt of the press office, responsible for herding the media to and from designated areas where they are covering the president. The wranglers are key members in Republican and Democrat administrations alike in keeping the president on schedule. EL-SAYED DRAGGED OVER ‘WEIRD’ FIXATION ON ‘TALKING ABOUT OTHER PEOPLE’S WIVES’ AFTER LATEST TRUMP ATTACK The clip and Rupar's commentary on it quickly went viral as users, including the White House, came out en masse to defend the young White House staffer and rail against the left-wing personality. The White House's rapid response X account responded to Rupar, who in recent weeks has repeatedly tracked and commented on the movements of embattled White House aide Natalie Harp. "This is a press wrangler doing her job — and doing it well. Aaron, meanwhile, is gutter trash (in his 40s) who spends his days hiding behind his keyboard and making disturbing comments about women doing their jobs. Truly a sick freak!" the White House account said. Following that response, Rupar whined online and suggested that the White House was inciting harassment and threats against him. "For the second straight day, the White House's taxpayer-funded incitement account is attacking me and oddly mentioning I'm in my 40s (which I know makes me way too old for the president) When they do this it results in a flood of harassing and threatening messages, which of course is the point," he said. DEM’S ‘SEXIST’ REMARK AGAINST CANCER SURVIVOR PROVOKES REPUBLICAN TO GO SCORCHED EARTH: ‘GUY’S GOT A PROBLEM’ Rupar found himself in the White House's crosshairs on Saturday, too, that time for posting another photo of Harp. He and other online leftist have been insinuating for weeks, without evidence, that Harp and Trump are engaged in an inappropriate relationship. "Look who made the trip to Ireland!" Rupar said in a post, adding a photo of Harp and a hashtag, #TravelWithNatalie, which he has used while tracking Harp's movements with Trump. The White House noted in its response that the president's aides, unsurprisingly, travel with him. "President Trump does, in fact, travel with staff. Aaron, on the other hand, is a sick, deluded freak (in his 40s) who sits behind a keyboard and posts creepy things like this," the post said. JON OSSOFF DODGES ON WHY HE INVOKED TRUMP AIDE'S NAME DURING GEORGIA CAMPAIGN RALLY Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., popularized the unsubstantiated gossip about Trump and Harp during a campaign speech last month. "He doesn’t want to do the job," Ossof said, referring to Trump. "He wants to build his ballroom and travel with Natalie on their apparently defenseless flying palace gifted by the emir of Qatar." articles.title: From 9/11 to burn pits, we must deal with long-term effects of toxic exposure
articles.summary: Marine veteran Joslin Joseph argues that the government failed to protect 9/11 responders and veterans from toxic exposure, highlighting the ongoing health crisis faced by those impacted by Ground Zero and burn pits.
articles.body:
Two days after 9/11 my buddy and I took a bus from our hometown in Clifton, N.J., and went into Manhattan. We wandered around the city and made our way south to what would later be called Ground Zero.

There were three things from that day that are seared into my memory. The first was the families of victims at the Manhattan Armory, carrying pictures of loved ones begging people to help them find their missing family and friends. The second was the smell. It was a combination of smoke, concrete, chemicals and batteries. The third was how bad it felt to breathe. I was a smoker at the time and told my buddy when we were making our way home that I felt like I just smoked a carton of cigarettes.

Years later, in Iraq, I had the ignominious duty of burning everything that was trash every single night. We burned everything to the point that it made zero sense. I was told that we didn’t want our trash to be sifted through by the enemy, so we had to burn everything. Plastic bottles, computers, batteries, paper, and all trash. When you dared ask if it was necessary or safe, you got chewed out.

In 2011, I was at the VA in San Diego to ask about a bump in my throat. The doctors found a lump on my thyroid. I asked if it had anything to do with my exposure to burn pits. They laughed at me and said no.

A couple of years later, the lump had doubled in size and had to be removed, along with half my thyroid. They had to conduct a sleep test before I could do surgery and found I had sleep apnea. I asked again if this and the growth had anything to do with exposure and was told no.

Around the same time, the brave men and women who worked around the clock at Ground Zero started coming down with similar yet more severe symptoms. They developed respiratory issues such as coughs, wheezing, shortness of breath and asthma. They would have sinus issues and reflux from their airways into the lungs. And some got cancer. Respiratory, blood, and lymph node cancers became prevalent.

Twenty-five years since the terror attacks on the U.S., and 25 years into what we labeled a “war on terror,” we have to come to terms with the fact that long term care for both 9/11 responders and Global War on Terrorism veterans is way more complex that what we thought it would be. We also knew but chose to ignore the fact that exposure would lead to long term effects.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani made news when he said that city officials at the time knew the air quality was bad but misled people by claiming it was safe. Of course, in the world we live in people couldn’t understand why he decided to come out and talk about this, calling it some type of conspiracy theory .

There is no conspiracy. The federal, state and local authorities knew there was asbestos, chemicals and toxins in the air. They said it was safe, based on regulations at the time. But they didn’t or wouldn’t factor in long term effects. It might be safe to be at Ground Zero for a day, like I was. But repeated days that went on for months? Surely, they had to know that wasn’t safe.

It was not a fair position to be in. Then-Mayor Rudy Guiliani had to get the city back to a sense of normalcy. New York isn’t just a normal run-of-the-mill city. It was and is the financial capital of the world. The clean up efforts had to happen as fast as possible.

That means there were hard decisions to be made. Yes, you had to look at the short-term needs which were very urgent. But leadership also means balancing the short-term needs with the long-term effects. And that is where the government failed us. Millions of dollars have been paid out to 9/11 responders, even though it has taken herculean efforts from advocates like Jon Stewart . And veterans are now getting help for their own exposure to burn pits, thanks to the PACT Act .

Despite this, there is still work to be done. Long term exposure is complex and we still don’t know how bad things will get. Countless more are starting to get symptoms as they get older. We know this because the same thing happened to Vietnam veterans when they were exposed to Agent Orange or Gulf War veterans when they had to breathe in smoke from oil well fires set by Saddam Hussein. The facts show this will be an ongoing issue. Last year, over 10,000 people were diagnosed with 9/11-related cancers .

Mamdani’s release of documents about air quality was needed. We must always look out for the long-term effects even when confronted with an urgent situation. And prepare for the long-term effects, including the financial needs of those who need help. We owe it to them to seek out the truth and advocate for their continued care, no matter the cost.

Joslin Joseph is a recipient of the Military Reporters and Editors award for Best Commentary-Opinion. A graduate of Harvard and Ohio State, he is a Marine veteran who served in Iraq. He currently lives in Anaheim, Calif.

articles.title: Manchin endorses Collins in Maine Senate race
articles.summary: Former Sen. Joe Manchin (I-W.Va.), a prominent centrist who left the Democratic Party at the end of his Senate career, has endorsed Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine), praising her as the “soul of the Senate.” Manchin gave his nod to Collins over Troy Jackson, her progressive challenger who supports “Medicare for All” and dismantling Immigration and…
articles.body:
Former Sen. Joe Manchin (I-W.Va.), a prominent centrist who left the Democratic Party at the end of his Senate career, has endorsed Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine), praising her as the “soul of the Senate.”

Manchin gave his nod to Collins over Troy Jackson, her progressive challenger who supports “Medicare for All” and dismantling Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

“You lose the Susan Collinses of the Senate, you’re losing the soul of the Senate — basically, a person you can talk to, who wants to do the right thing all of the time. Now, everybody says, “Oh, she doesn’t do this, doesn’t speak up.” Susan is always in there, always in the trenches,” Manchin said Monday on CNBC.

Manchin and Collins worked closely together on an array of bipartisan initiatives, including the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act in 2021, a massive infrastructure bill, and the Bipartisan Safer Communities Act in 2022, which established a red-flag program to counter gun violence.

“Joe is a dear friend and trusted colleague with whom I have always worked closely to solve problems and deliver results for the people of Maine and America,” Collins said in a statement.

“From helping end government shutdowns and negotiating the Electoral Count Act to delivering COVID relief and historic investments in our nation’s infrastructure, we have shown what is possible when Republicans and Democrats work together to find common ground and get things done. I am honored to have his support,” she said.

Manchin has recoiled at the idea of supporting candidates aligned with the Democratic Socialists of America.

He told CBS’s Margaret Brennan, the host of “Face the Nation,” last month that there’s “no way” he would support a socialist candidate.

“Even if they have some good ideas?” Brennan asked.

“I’ll support the good ideas, but how could you support some of the crazy stuff they’re for? Have you seen their platform?” Manchin responded.

Jackson does not identify as a democratic socialist, but he has received the support of Democratic socialists, just as Graham Platner, whom Jackson replaced as the Democratic nominee in Maine, did before dropping his bid for Senate.

Manchin left the Democratic Party in May 2024 to register as an independent.

He frequently clashed with progressive Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) over the size of former President Biden’s Build Back Better agenda and repeatedly warned Democratic colleagues that excessive spending would fuel inflation.

articles.title: Lowering gas prices requires stopping climate shakedowns
articles.summary: President Trump met with oil refiners to discuss expanding capacity, but analysts suggest that lowering gasoline prices requires legislative action to block state climate lawsuits and foreign regulations.
articles.body:
On Sept. 1, just as the national average for gasoline hit $4.09 a gallon , President Trump brought oil refiners and fuel distributors to the White House to discuss expanding refining capacity and bringing prices down. Administration officials said the conversation included “concrete ways to expand capacity, including regulation changes, faster permitting and additional investments.”

Removing federal barriers to new projects is a good place to start, as American refineries are already operating at nearly 97 percent of capacity. But permits alone will only go so far. Unless something is done to stop state governments and foreign regulators from sabotaging American energy dominance, the price at the pump, not to mention U.S. national security, will suffer.

In blue states and municipalities here in the United States, an unholy alliance of progressive officials and their cabal of climate litigators have weaponized climate lawsuits and “Climate Superfunds” to bleed the industry of billions of dollars. Meanwhile, across the Atlantic, European regulators are forcing costly climate mandates into American supply chains.

Together, these forces are inflicting an unnecessary burden on our energy industry at a time when U.S. energy dominance matters most. All of this raises costs that get passed on to consumers and makes new refinery investments harder to justify. Any serious effort to lower gas prices and expand refining capacity has to stop the lawsuits, retroactive charges, and foreign mandates driving rising costs.

To Trump’s credit, his executive order last year directed the Justice Department to identify and challenge ideologically motivated state laws burdening domestic energy production. His administration has since challenged New York’s and Vermont’s “Climate Superfund” laws as well as climate actions in Hawaii and Michigan. That pushback paid off last month when a federal judge blocked the New York superfund, which sought $75 billion in retroactive charges against oil and gas companies based on fossil fuels legally produced and sold between 2000 and 2018.

Vermont’s Climate Superfund, however, remains very much alive, and other states could easily pass their own versions.

Beyond the climate superfund laws, blue states and municipalities are also bleeding energy companies dry in court over damages tied to decades of global emissions. California alone sued five major oil companies and the American Petroleum Institute in 2023 for allegedly “deceiving the public about climate change,” while Multnomah County, Ore., is seeking nearly $52 billion from oil and gas companies over the 2021 heat wave. Hawaii filed one last year alleging “harm to public trust resources,” while Michigan filed this year, accusing the industry of a “conspiracy” to “restrict the development of renewable energy and electric vehicles.”

Whatever the theory, these lawsuits force a handful of American energy companies to spend millions defending themselves in local courts, while losing even a few could expose the industry to hundreds of billions in liability and allow local courts to set energy policy for the rest of the country.

Rather than leave energy companies and the Justice Department to keep fighting the same battle one state and one courtroom at a time, Trump can and should put his full weight behind Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) and Rep. Harriet Hageman’s (R-Wyo.) Stop Climate Shakedowns Act . The legislation would prohibit climate lawsuits in state and federal court and void state energy-penalty laws such as the climate superfunds.

But even then, the administration must still deal with our friends across the Atlantic, where the European Union is using its Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive to require American companies that operate there to police environmental practices throughout their entire supply chains under the threat of fines.

As Rep. Craig Goldman (R-Texas) has noted, a gas-station owner in Fort Worth could get pulled into Europe’s mandates simply because his franchise agreement is with an American fuel company that operates there. The owner does no business in Europe and has no representation there, and yet he could still get stuck paying the compliance costs Europe adds to his contract.

Fortunately, a solution is waiting in the wings here too. The PROTECT USA Act, now before Congress, would stop foreign governments from forcing their sustainability rules on American companies. Goldman’s Stop the EU Overreach Act would also direct the U.S. trade representative to investigate whether the EU directives unfairly restrict American businesses and determine how the United States should respond. Trump should do everything in his power to push both forward alongside the Stop Climate Shakedowns Act.

Pressing refiners to expand capacity should absolutely be part of Trump’s effort to lower gasoline prices. But faster permits and regulatory relief will not be enough to justify billion-dollar investments while blue states pursue retroactive climate charges and European regulators add new costs to American supply chains.

If the administration wants refiners to invest and consumers to pay less, it must stop hostile governments from piling new costs onto American energy companies.

Jason Isaac is the CEO of the American Energy Institute. He previously served four terms in the Texas House of Representatives.

articles.title: WATCH: Talarico instantly names favorite Texas drag queen — a performer who says he ‘works with children’
articles.summary: James Talarico instantly named Alyssa Edwards as his favorite Texas drag queen, spotlighting a performer who has publicly discussed working with children.
articles.body: EXCLUSIVE: Texas Democratic Senate hopeful James Talarico instantly named Alyssa Edwards when asked at a campaign event to identify his favorite drag queen in the state — pointing to someone who has publicly described himself as "a drag performer that works with children." Talarico’s past comments on sexuality and gender issues have become a line of attack in the Senate race, including his remark that "God is nonbinary" and his 2023 praise for Texas having "some of the best drag queens in the nation." "Mr. Talarico, so nice to meet you... I was there when you defended the drags," video shows a man telling the Democratic nominee as he approached to take a photo together at the event. JAMES TALARICO ADMITS PAST COMMENTS 'MISSED THE MARK' WHEN CONFRONTED ON CLAIMS LIKE GOD IS 'NON-BINARY' "Who’s your favorite drag queen in Texas?" the man asks in the video. Without a pause, Talarico responds: "Oh, my gosh. Probably Alyssa Edwards." The exchange comes after the Washington Free Beacon reported on a 2021 event Talarico headlined called "Taylor PRIDE" in Taylor, Texas, where an 11-year-old boy performed in drag under the name Kween Kee Kee. In the more recent exchange, Talarico's instant response naming Edwards referred to Justin Dwayne Lee Johnson, whose stage name is Alyssa Edwards. Johnson has been an outspoken advocate for youth drag shows. IOWA TEACHERS SUSPENDED OVER VIRAL STUDENT-RUN DRAG SHOW REACH SETTLEMENT BEFORE TRIAL "I remember being at World Pride in New York a few years back and sharing the stage with my dance students, one of the most powerful moments of my life," Johnson said in an interview with Out magazine. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER Johnson’s work with young dancers was also featured in the 2018 Netflix docuseries "Dancing Queen." The Dallas Observer reported that Johnson called one 10-year-old male student his "mini-me," and that the child dressed as Alyssa Edwards during an episode of the series. When asked about the encounter, a spokesperson for Talarico instead appeared to turn the criticism toward the Republican opponent: "James’ favorite performer is Ken Paxton — who dresses up as attorney general while giving sweetheart deals to child sex predators," Talarico campaign spokesperson JT Ennis told Fox News Digital. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News Digital also reached out to Johnson’s representation for comment. Asked separately by Fox News last week about his controversial comments on gender and related issues, Talarico said he "missed the mark on some of my past statements." He said then that he no longer believes there are six sexes, and that people are bringing up that kind of commentary because they do not want to talk about "six dollar diesel" with Republicans in the majority. Fox News' Brooke Taylor contributed to this report.

articles.title: Reporter’s Notebook: Congress meets AI as fears of human extinction jolt Capitol Hill
articles.summary: Members of Congress are in freakout mode over AI after OpenAI agents escaped isolation and hacked Hugging Face, sparking urgent regulation calls.
articles.body: Members of Congress returned to Capitol Hill this week in pure freakout mode. There are apocalyptic scenarios about AI seizing control of water systems. Subways. Air traffic control. Crashing planes. Firing nuclear weapons. Even sending Prince Harry and Meghan Markle back to the United States. But seriously, there’s real fear that Congress may be running behind on regulating AI. And there are concerns that AI might be developing at such a rapid clip that it’s too late to harness the technology. Suspicion about data centers has long percolated among voters. Then former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon declared that AI could extinguish humankind within a decade. This came after a swarm of OpenAI agents independently "escaped" isolation – then leveraged security vulnerabilities to hack the artificial intelligence platform Hugging Face. The AI agents weren’t supposed to be capable of any of that. Researchers say they even used covert methods to communicate with each other via a special language. AI EXTINCTION WARNINGS DOMINATE HEADLINES AFTER EX—ANTHROPIC EMPLOYEE'S VIRAL POST "My phone has been ringing off the hook from a lot of colleagues who really saw the news of the whistleblower as a tipping point," said Rep. Lori Trahan, D-Mass., who has toiled on bipartisan AI legislation. "Then people hear the words ‘human extinction.’ When they hear loss of control. When they hear ‘catastrophic risk,’ I think (people) are waking up and they're saying, ‘Where the hell is Congress?’" "It's not like we've been sitting on our hands here," said Rep. Jay Obernolte, R-Calif., an AI expert who’s worked on bipartisan AI guardrails with Trahan. "I don't think it's fair to say that there's been a reluctance to act. It's just that the wheels of progress turn very slowly in Congress." Congress, meet AI. AI, meet Congress. FOX NEWS POLL: VOTERS SEE AI REGULATION AS URGENT, RANK SAFEGUARDS AHEAD OF INNOVATION Is this like lawmakers trying to make sense of this new-fangled invention called the internet – or "information superhighway" – back in the 1990s? When it comes to technological innovation, Congress has rarely been ahead of it. AI is no exception. OpenAI founder Sam Altman has visited Capitol Hill on at least five occasions between 2023 and today. He met with House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., and Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., as recently as June. "This is sort of an important, urgent and in some ways unprecedented moment and I think we really need the government to lead," Altman said during one trip to Capitol Hill in 2023. When Democrats were in the majority between 2023 and 2025, Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., convened regular bipartisan symposia on AI at the Capitol for all senators. He hauled in Altman. Elon Musk. Mark Zuckerberg. Bill Gates. Anyone who could educate lawmakers about AI and what they should do about it. Schumer hoped that senators would develop their own ideas about how to legislate on AI and have a measure ready. He wasn’t dictating what they should do from his post. "Our timetable in terms of producing legislation is not years, and not days and weeks. But months,’ said Schumer on July 11, 2023. "It can't be days or weeks. But nor should it be years. It will be in the general category of months," said Schumer on Sept. 13, 2023. "We're already sitting down and trying to figure out legislation. It won't be easy. But I still say months. Not days. Not years," said Schumer on Nov. 29, 2023. OBAMA PRIVATELY SOUNDS ALARM ON ‘DANGEROUS’ AI, URGES DEMOCRATS TO PUT ISSUE AT CENTER OF AGENDA Schumer along with Sens. Mike Rounds, R-S.D., Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., and Todd Young, R-Ind., produced the document "Driving U.S. Innovation In Artificial Intelligence: A Roadmap for Artificial Intelligence Policy in the United States Senate" in May 2024. There was hope the House and Senate might latch some provisions of the package onto a must-pass bill in the fall of 2024. But it went nowhere. "Chuck Schumer and I see the world with very different lenses. He always wants to have a growth of government approach to everything," said Johnson in a September 2024, interview with yours truly. "I think the reaction, or the knee-jerk reaction, perhaps, of the Senate would be to just go in and overlay this with red tape. And we're not going to do that in the House." AI KILL SWITCH BILL COULD SHUT DOWN ROGUE MODELS Now a group of Democrats is imploring Johnson to keep the House in session this fall until it adopts "meaningful AI safeguards." Rep. Sam Liccardo, D-Calif., says "urgent action" is necessary to impede AI from spiraling out of control. "We need to do it fast, because otherwise this can be very dangerous," said Rep. Suhas Subramanyam, D-Va. Despite the apprehension, it’s far from clear that Congress will move right away. But Obernolte believes these AI incidents could spark action. "I think that this increases not only visibility, but the sense of urgency in getting a federal regulatory framework passed this year," said Obernolte. "I do think it is that dire," said Rep. Don Beyer, D-Va., who is pursuing a master’s degree in AI at George Mason University. But truly, what power could lawmakers have over AI? "Because it's so new, we don't actually know what kind of legislation will fix it," said Beyer. "So I think we're going to introduce imperfect and pass imperfect legislation, see what it does, and then learn as we go." Kind of like AI, learning and developing as it goes. However, how universal is the congressional "large language model?" And is Congress truly nimble enough to keep pace with AI? Obernolte says the headstrong AI agents hacked out of their controlled environment because the model "intentionally had its safety controls removed." This is kind of like testing any new technology just to see what it’s capable of. But the question is whether AI could eventually outwit the developers and evade restrictions? Obernolte says AI engineers and lawmakers are also up against something else: pop culture and science fiction. "The Matrix." "War Games." The Terminator movies. TRUMP UNLOADS ON TECH TITANS PUSHING FOR SLOWDOWN ON EMERGING INDUSTRY: ‘WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS!’ "You don't start with something out of a Terminator movie where an army of evil robots rises up to take over the world," said Obernolte. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP At a recent town hall meeting, the California Republican says an elderly woman asked him if AI was so dangerous, why Congress doesn’t just ban it. "I thought my head was going to explode. And I realized that we'd spent an hour talking about all the bad stuff and we hadn't talked at all about the good stuff," said Obernolte. There’s certainly a perception issue. And if Congress views AI as a threat, lawmakers will legislate in a way to protect constituents against the threat. But lawmakers aren’t ready to tackle this. Despite recent developments, don’t expect anything major until later this year or early next. After all, lawmakers are focused elsewhere. The midterm elections are approaching. This session of Congress is nearing its conclusion. And just like Arnold Schwarzenegger said in "Terminator 2," lawmakers are ready to declare "Hasta la vista, baby."

articles.title: Sydney Sweeney criticized by women athletes for nude sports prediction market ad
articles.summary: Actress Sydney Sweeney is facing criticism from a growing number of female athletes online over a new advertisement for a sports prediction market platform in which she appears wearing little or no clothing. The advertisement, promoting prediction market platform NoVig, opens with a nude Sweeney asking the camera “think you know sports? Prove it,” while…
articles.body:
Actress Sydney Sweeney is facing criticism from a growing number of female athletes online over a new advertisement for a sports prediction market platform in which she appears wearing little or no clothing.

The advertisement, promoting prediction market platform NoVig, opens with a nude Sweeney asking the camera “think you know sports? Prove it,” while holding two footballs in front of her chest.

In another series of shots, Sweeney sits atop a basketball hoop, crouches in front of a hockey goal keeper’s net and lies on a soccer bench, all with limited or no clothing on.

Several female professional athletes, across a wide array of sports, are expressing outrage at the less than one-minute ad, arguing it objectifies women in sports and is in poor taste.

“idk what Sydney Sweeney was doing but this is what a women in sports looks like,” the American gymnast Gracie Kramer wrote in one post on Instagram , which she captioned “because it really is that deep.”

Skye Nicolson, an Australian professional boxer wrote Sweeney was “giving the ad campaign exactly what they wanted, but honestly these companies need to do better.”

Australian surfer Felicity Palmateer told CNN she found the ad to be “very damaging” for female athletes.

“Just absolute utter disbelief, incredibly disappointing, like, how far you can put women’s sports backwards in the space of a 42-second commercial,” Palmateer said.

Sweeney has not commented publicly on the backlash the ad is receiving, but she reportedly approached NoVig about participating in the ad and the company’s CEO told Front Office Sports she was “great at captivating audiences and being the center of attention.”

The actress has been at the center of controversy in the past, most recently in connection with an advertisement for American Eagle jeans which some critics said smacked of promoting eugenics.

Sweeney told Variety at the time of her work promoting various brands, “I’ve always believed that I’m not here to tell people what to think.”

articles.title: Democrat Al Green to force House-wide vote on impeaching Trump
articles.summary: House Democratic Rep. Al Green is mounting yet another effort to impeach President Donald Trump, he announced on Monday.
articles.body: Longtime Rep. Al Green, D-Texas, announced on Monday that he intends to force a vote on impeaching President Donald Trump, citing federal immigration officers' killing of two U.S. citizens earlier this year. Green, who has publicly protested Trump on multiple occasions, introduced what's called a privileged resolution on the House floor aimed at booting the president out of office. A privileged resolution is a mechanism that allows any lawmaker to force the entire chamber to consider a bill within two legislative days. That means House GOP leaders will have to hold a vote on the measure by the end of the day on Wednesday. TRUMP COULD FACE IMPEACHMENT IF DEMOCRATS SEIZE HOUSE MAJORITY, GOP LEADER WARNS The vote is all but guaranteed to be a political headache for Democrats who are fighting to take back the House and Senate in the November midterm elections. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., has long demurred on the subject of impeachment, maintaining that Democrats are focused on tackling issues like high living costs that are critical to everyday Americans. JEFFRIES BRAGS ABOUT DEM OBSTRUCTION AGAINST TRUMP AS HE DEFENDS KUSHNER MEETING He and 127 other House Democrats voted with Republicans to quash a previous Trump impeachment effort by Green in June 2025. But the latest effort could be his last public demonstration against Trump after the 79-year-old progressive lost his primary to a younger Democrat calling for generational change. CONSERVATIVES ERUPT AFTER AL GREEN MELTS DOWN DURING VIRAL CLASH: 'UNHINGED LUNATIC' Green was also notably thrown out of both of Trump's addresses to a joint session of Congress during this term. During his first address since returning to the White House, Green repeatedly waved his cane at Trump and shouted while the president spoke. At the beginning of Trump's State of the Union address earlier this year, Green held up a sign that said, "Black People Aren't Apes." Democratic leaders have signaled they are preparing for a flurry of investigations into the Trump administration and the president's circle if they win the midterms in November. Green insisted that Democrats did not need to wait for those probes, however, demanding in a letter to House colleagues that a vote on impeaching Trump is held immediately. "To those who say, 'Wait until next year' and 'Buckle up' when the investigations start, I say: How many more lives must we lose, and how many more loved ones of victims have to plead for help before the self-evident evidence from videos and President Trump’s own words compel us to act?" Green wrote. "The available overwhelming evidence sufficiently demonstrates that President Trump is unfit and dangerous to our democracy." The latest impeachment resolution calls Trump "a great threat to democracy and the Constitution for current high crimes and misdemeanors."
